issues.legal_issue: A scheme-making procedure for a religious institution that provides for judicial inquiry and an appeal to a court does not impose an unreasonable restriction on the head of the institution’s property rights.
material_facts: The challenged law required an initial inquiry by an Assistant Commissioner holding judicial office, followed by an inquiry by a Commissioner who was a judicial officer of at least the rank of a Subordinate Judge.
The Commissioner’s inquiry was, so far as applicable, to follow the Code of Civil Procedure rules for the trial of suits.
The law provided an appeal to the High Court in broad terms, permitting challenges on facts and law.
The earlier procedure had been invalidated because an executive officer could settle a scheme without judicial intervention or a right of appeal.
issues.conclusion: The scheme-making provisions were not unconstitutional as unreasonable restrictions on the heads’ property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects the property interest of a head of a Math, although reasonable restrictions may be imposed in the public interest. A scheme-making process is not an unreasonable restriction merely because the initial decision is made by a Commissioner rather than through a separate civil suit, if the affected person can present the case in a judicial inquiry and has a regular appeal to a court. The Court applied Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Math ([1954] S.C.R. 1005) and distinguished Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_procedure and judicial_officers_conduct_the_inquiries and inquiry_follows_civil_trial_procedure and broad_court_appeal_is_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_proce: A person challenges the constitutionality of a process for settling a scheme for a religious institution.
predicates.judicial_officers_conduct_the_inquiries: The preliminary and principal inquiries are conducted by officers holding judicial office.
predicates.inquiry_follows_civil_trial_procedure: The principal inquiry follows, so far as applicable, the procedures used in a civil trial.
predicates.broad_court_appeal_is_available: An affected person can appeal to a court on factual and legal grounds.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to a scheme procedure involves inquiries by judicial officers conducted under civil-trial procedures and a broad court appeal, the procedure is not treated as an unreasonable property restriction.

issues.legal_issue: A short appeal period and the absence of an automatic stay of a scheme do not make the scheme-making process an unreasonable restriction when the appeal can be pursued without court fees where appropriate and the appellate court can provide necessary financial assistance.
material_facts: An appeal had to be brought within a shorter period than the period previously allowed for a suit.
The Commissioner’s order took effect while an appeal was pending.
The Court noted that an appellant unable to pay could use the procedure for appealing in forma pauperis.
The State accepted that the appellate court had discretion to direct the provision of funds from the trust estate for the appeal or for interim maintenance.
issues.conclusion: The appeal period and the absence of an automatic stay did not render the scheme-making provisions unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(f), procedural restrictions are assessed in light of the practical ability to present an appeal. The possibility of proceeding in forma pauperis and the appellate court’s inherent discretion to prevent the appeal from becoming illusory supported the conclusion that the restrictions were not unreasonable. This reasoning formed part of the Court’s application of Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Math ([1954] S.C.R. 1005) and Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_appeal_conditions and appeal_period_is_short and order_operates_during_appeal and fee_waiver_route_is_available and appellate_court_can_provide_interim_support

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheme_appea: A person challenges the constitutionality of the conditions governing an appeal from a scheme order.
predicates.appeal_period_is_short: The time allowed to appeal is comparatively short.
predicates.order_operates_during_appeal: The challenged order remains operative while the appeal is pending.
predicates.fee_waiver_route_is_available: A person unable to pay can pursue the appeal without paying the ordinary court fees.
predicates.appellate_court_can_provide_interim_supp: The appellate court has discretion to provide funds needed to conduct the appeal or meet interim maintenance needs.

issues.definition: When an appeal period is short and the order remains operative, the conditions are not treated as an unreasonable property restriction if fee relief is available and the appellate court can provide necessary interim support.

issues.legal_issue: The legislature may deem previously framed schemes to have been settled under a later law, while providing a new appeal, without impermissibly overriding a judicial determination of unconstitutionality or impairing access to constitutional remedies.
material_facts: Schemes had been framed under an earlier law during a period when the procedure lacked the judicial appeal later required by the Court’s ruling.
The legislature provided that the schemes would be treated as settled under the later law and gave affected persons an appeal to the High Court.
The provision did not deem the schemes valid under the earlier law as it then stood; it treated them as schemes under the later law.
The affected persons remained able to seek relief under Article 32, and the petitions were considered on their merits.
issues.conclusion: The provision deeming the earlier schemes to have been settled under the later law was within legislative competence and did not improperly interfere with the Court’s jurisdiction or the right to seek relief under Article 32.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature cannot override unconstitutionality by declaring a measure valid under the law that existed when it was made. It may, however, enact a competent new law that adopts prior acts by deeming them to have been taken under that new law, subject to the new law’s procedures and remedies. Such legislation does not take away the Article 32 remedy merely because the legal basis for an earlier constitutional challenge has been changed. The Court applied Article 32 and distinguished the invalidity ruling in Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_adoption_of_prior_schemes and prior_schemes_were_given_new_legal_basis and appeal_under_new_law_is_available and constitutional_remedy_remains_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_: A person challenges a law that adopts previously framed schemes by deeming them to have been made under a later legal regime.
predicates.prior_schemes_were_given_new_legal_basis: The law treats the earlier schemes as having been settled under the new regime rather than as valid under the former regime when they were made.
predicates.appeal_under_new_law_is_available: The law provides an appeal against an adopted scheme under the new regime.
predicates.constitutional_remedy_remains_available: A person remains able to seek a constitutional remedy against the adopted scheme.

issues.definition: When a law gives prior schemes a new legal basis, provides an appeal under that basis, and leaves constitutional relief available, the adoption is within legislative competence and does not bar constitutional relief.

issues.legal_issue: Deeming previously framed schemes to have been settled under a later law does not impose an unreasonable property restriction when the affected persons retain an appeal and the earlier proceedings provided substantially equivalent safeguards.
material_facts: The later law provided a right of appeal against the schemes and allowed a period to bring that appeal.
Although the earlier procedure did not include a preliminary inquiry by an Assistant Commissioner, the schemes had in fact been settled by a judicial officer.
The procedure actually followed under the earlier rules was consistent with the civil-trial procedure used under the later law.
The earlier schemes had been framed jointly by the Commissioner and one or more government officers, providing a safeguard absent from the later procedure.
issues.conclusion: The deeming provision did not place the affected persons at a substantial procedural disadvantage and was not an unreasonable restriction on their property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) requires consideration of whether the procedure, taken as a whole, unreasonably restricts the protected property interest. A deeming provision is not unreasonable merely because it does not reproduce every procedural step of the later law where a court appeal is provided and the actual earlier proceedings had substantially equivalent safeguards. The Court applied the principles in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Math ([1954] S.C.R. 1005) and Mahant Sri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa ([1954] S.C.R. 1046).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_deemed_schem: A person challenges a law that treats schemes framed under an earlier regime as having been settled under a later regime.
predicates.appeal_is_available: An affected person can appeal against the scheme to a court.
predicates.earlier_inquiry_was_conducted_by_judicia: The officer who conducted the earlier scheme inquiry held judicial office.
predicates.earlier_procedure_followed_civil_trial_p: The procedure actually used in the earlier inquiry was consistent with civil-trial practice.
predicates.earlier_process_had_additional_participa: The earlier scheme process included participation by one or more additional officials alongside the decision-maker.

issues.definition: When a challenge to deemed schemes concerns a process that allowed a court appeal and the earlier inquiry used judicial and civil-trial safeguards with additional participation, the deeming provision is not treated as an unreasonable property restriction.
